doc.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Amplification and electronics in jazz
summary: Jacobs and Harris dislike microphones on instruments and electronics; Armstrong said he loves change unless it makes things worse.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Phoebe, as a fan of the music, was there time periods when new things were happening that you started to question like —

Oh my goodness yes. I mean I absolutely was horrified to think that people would use six microphones in Carnegie Hall and attach microphones to instruments, to electrify them. The distortion of sound disturbed me terribly. I couldn’t bear it. And also to listen to the way people are playing music these days, the amount of volume, they take all the beauty out of the music. I know when Duke Ellington recorded at Carnegie Hall or Benny Goodman, they used one microphone. Pops only used one microphone. Carnegie Hall is such a wonderful hall of sound so the whole transition of like a Herbie Alpert — he’s the first one, isn’t he, that put the microphone in his trumpet — oh my God. I just couldn’t bear that.
Yeah it takes the balancing between the group, it takes it out of the musician’s hands and gives it to a sound man.

Right, right. I mean that’s what it is. And I’ll tell you, I’m like Phoebe, the microphones — she can’t take the microphones but when I walk into a concert hall and I see a bunch of computers on the stage it’s — you know my thought is well do they need all of that to create music? And so if they need that what do you say about the playing? You know? And people, we all hear it all at the same time. You know what I’m saying? So it’s not — they’re not going to be judged on the effectiveness of their electronic equipment.

You know what Pops had to say about that? He said he loves change because change represents progress. But when change takes something good and makes it worse, forget about it, he don’t want to have nothing to do with it. That was good enough for me.
